title: The Eolian harp
greek: Greek Aiolos, god of the winds
short: An Aeolian harp is a stringed box set in a window for the wind to play; the poem makes it a model of mind and nature.
body: Named after Aeolus, keeper of the winds, the instrument was fashionable in eighteenth-century houses; James Thomson wrote an 'Ode on Aeolus's Harp' (1748) and described one in The Castle of Indolence. Placed 'length-ways in the clasping casement', it sounds without a player as the breeze varies, producing chords that rise and fall unpredictably. For Coleridge and later Romantics it became the classic image of a passive receiver animated by an outside power: the poet's mind moved by impressions, or all living things moved by one divine breath. The poem's argument turns on how far that image can be pressed.

title: My pensive Sara
short: Sara Fricker, whom Coleridge married on 4 October 1795; the poem dates from their courtship and early marriage at a cottage in Clevedon, Somerset.
body: A manuscript version is dated 20 August 1795 at Clevedon, on the Bristol Channel, and the poem was published in Poems on Various Subjects (1796) as 'Effusion XXXV', with the note 'Composed August 20th, 1795, At Clevedon, Somersetshire'. Coleridge married Sara that October, and the couple spent their honeymoon in the rose-covered cottage. Sara is addressed throughout but never speaks; her 'more serious eye' finally rebukes the speaker's speculations. The marriage later failed, which colours biographical readings of the domestic peace the poem celebrates.

anchor: Meet emblems they of Innocence and Love
title: Jasmin ... Myrtle ... emblems
short: White jasmine signifies innocence, and myrtle, sacred to Venus, love; the cottage is framed in the emblematic language of flowers.
body: In classical tradition the myrtle was Venus's plant and was used in wedding garlands, while white flowers such as jasmine stood for purity. 'Meet' means fitting. The parenthesis, like the later '(such should wisdom be)' of the evening star, shows the young poet moralising the landscape as he describes it, a habit the poem's ending will question. The scents 'Snatched from yon bean-field' and the hushed world complete a scene of domestic and natural harmony.

title: the star of eve / Serenely brilliant
short: The evening star (Venus, Hesperus) shines 'opposite' the sunset; the poet's aside makes it a model of wisdom.
body: As the clouds lose the sunset light, the evening star appears; Coleridge's parenthesis '(such should wisdom be)' compares its calm brilliance to the ideal of wisdom, serene rather than flashy. The detail also places the poem precisely at dusk. Venus as evening star is the planet of love, linking with the myrtle of l. 4. The small moral asides of the opening paragraph show the poet already turning sense-impressions into meanings, a habit the poem pursues on a grand scale in the harp passages and then rebukes at the end.

title: The stilly murmur of the distant sea / Tells us of silence
short: The faint murmur of the sea makes silence audible; the short broken line enacts the pause.
body: 'Stilly' is a poetic adjective meaning quiet or calm. The paradox is that the faint sound makes the surrounding silence perceptible, a sensory subtlety typical of the conversation poems. The line is left incomplete and the verse paragraph breaks, so that the page itself gives a silence before the harp is introduced. Coleridge's later poems repeatedly use such natural sounds at the edge of hearing, as in 'Frost at Midnight'.

anchor: Like some coy maid half yielding to her lover
title: Like some coy maid half yielding to her lover
short: The breeze caresses the harp like a lover, and its music is the 'sweet upbraiding' of a half-willing maid; the simile is frankly erotic.
body: The harp's response to the wind is imagined as a courtship: the 'desultory' (fitful, wandering) breeze caresses it, and the strings reproach it so sweetly as to tempt a repetition of 'the wrong'. In a poem addressed to a new bride, the image is playful and sensuous. Critics note that it prepares the passive model of the mind in the later sections, in which thoughts 'Traverse my indolent and passive brain' as the breeze moves the strings.

title: sequacious
short: 'Sequacious' means following one another in sequence; the long notes swell and fall like waves.
body: From Latin sequax, 'inclined to follow', the word appears in Dryden's 'Song for St Cecilia's Day' (1687), where trees uprooted 'sequacious of the lyre' follow Orpheus. Coleridge's notes follow one another in continuous succession, and 'Over delicious surges sink and rise' gives them the movement of the sea. The passage then turns to fairy imagery, elfins voyaging on gales from Fairy-Land, and to birds of paradise.

title: Footless and wild, like birds of Paradise
short: Early European specimens of birds of paradise arrived without feet, and legend held that they had none and never landed, living always in flight.
body: Traders in New Guinea removed the feet of the skins sent to Europe, which gave rise to the belief that the birds were footless, lived on air and dew, and never alighted; Linnaeus named one species Paradisaea apoda, 'footless'. Coleridge's melodies, like the birds, never 'pause, nor perch' but hover 'on untamed wing'. The image of perpetual, unsettled motion suits both the harp's music and the speculative mind that the end of the poem will check.

sources.cite: Ernest Hartley Coleridge, ed., The Complete Poetical Works of Samuel Taylor Coleridge (Oxford, 1912), vol. I, 'The Eolian Harp', textual notes

anchor: O! the one life within us and abroad
title: O! the one life within us and abroad
short: The famous lines on 'the one life' in all things were added in 1817, more than twenty years after the poem's composition.
body: The passage first appeared in the errata to Sibylline Leaves (1817); the earlier texts went straight from the birds of paradise to the speaker on the hillside. It states the vision of a single life in mind and world, a 'light in sound' and 'sound-like power in light', which Abrams related to contemporary physics of light and sound and to Coleridge's later philosophy. Because the lines are late, critics debate their effect: they make the pantheistic idea more joyous and more central, and so make Sara's rebuke at the end harder to accept as final. Students should cite the poem as revised in 1817 and note the addition.

anchor: Traverse my indolent and passive brain
title: my indolent and passive brain
short: The poet's thoughts come 'uncalled and undetained', like gales over the harp: the mind as a passive instrument, an idea close to Hartley's associationism.
body: In 1795 Coleridge was an admirer of David Hartley, whose Observations on Man (1749) explained thought as the association of sensations transmitted by vibrations in the nerves; he named his first son Hartley in 1796. The image of the brain as a 'subject lute' (an instrument subject to the wind) fits this mechanistic psychology. Coleridge's later criticism, especially in Biographia Literaria (1817), rejected the passive model in favour of an active imagination, so the passage is often read as recording a position he outgrew.

anchor: Be but organic harps diversely framed
title: organic harps diversely framed
short: The speculation proper: all living things may be harps of different construction, played into thought by one breeze that is both the soul of each and God of all.
body: The hypothetical 'what if' extends the harp image to all 'animated nature'. 'Organic' here means having organs, living. The 'intellectual breeze' that sweeps over them is a single universal mind, 'At once the Soul of each, and God of all'. The idea comes close to pantheism, and editors have compared Spinoza and the Neoplatonists as well as Priestley's Unitarian thought, which Coleridge then shared. The question form keeps the speculation tentative, but it is exactly the kind of thought Sara's look rebukes.

title: Plastic
short: 'Plastic' means shaping or formative, as in Ralph Cudworth's 'plastic nature', a creative force that moulds matter.
body: The word does not mean malleable here but actively forming. The Cambridge Platonist Ralph Cudworth, in The True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678), argued for a 'plastic nature', a power through which God shapes the world without intervening at every point; Coleridge read Cudworth closely in the mid-1790s, and Bristol Library borrowing records are usually cited for this. The breeze thus shapes the harps it plays, and the passage blends Cudworth's Platonism with the more materialist necessitarianism of Hartley and Priestley.

title: biddest me walk humbly with my God
short: Sara's 'mild reproof' calls the speaker back to orthodox humility, in the words of Micah 6:8; the speculations become 'unhallowed'.
body: Micah 6:8 asks what the LORD requires but 'to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God'. Sara, 'Meek daughter in the family of Christ', speaks only through her eye and through the scriptural phrase the speaker gives her. The poet now calls his ideas 'shapings of the unregenerate mind', 'Bubbles' on the spring of 'vain Philosophy'. Critics disagree about the retraction. Some take it as sincere piety; others see it as social and domestic deference that does not refute the vision, or as a sign of Coleridge's lifelong struggle between speculative philosophy and Christian faith. The 1817 addition of the 'one life' lines intensified this tension.

title: The Incomprehensible
short: God as 'incomprehensible', beyond human understanding, echoes the Athanasian Creed in the Book of Common Prayer ('The Father incomprehensible ...').
body: The Creed of St Athanasius, appointed to be said in the Church of England's Book of Common Prayer, declares the Father, Son and Holy Ghost 'incomprehensible', in the older sense of 'not to be contained or limited'. Coleridge, then a Unitarian who rejected the Trinity, nonetheless uses its language to rebuke his own speculation: God can be spoken of only 'with awe' and with 'Faith that inly feels'. The closing lines turn to personal salvation and domestic thanks, 'Peace, and this cot, and thee, dear honoured Maid!', returning to the cottage of the opening.

anchor: Methinks, it should have been impossible
title: Conversation poem
short: Blank verse in a relaxed, speaking voice addressed to a silent listener: the first of Coleridge's 'conversation poems', with a circling structure that returns home.
body: The term 'conversation poem' was popularised by George McLean Harper in 1925, from Coleridge's subtitle for 'The Nightingale: A Conversation Poem' (1798). The group includes 'This Lime-Tree Bower', 'Frost at Midnight' and 'Fears in Solitude'. Typically the poem begins in a quiet present scene, rises through meditation to a large speculative or visionary moment, and returns to the scene and the addressee. 'The Eolian Harp' shows the pattern clearly, from the cottage to the 'one intellectual breeze' and back to 'this cot'. The informal syntax, with exclamations and parentheses, is part of the effect.
